profile.summary: Daniel presents the tension between the exile of Judah and the faithfulness of God to his promises. Set in the Babylonian domain and at the beginning of the restoration under Cyrus, the book shows Daniel and his friends preserving his identity as the Lord's people amid cultural pressure, the political threat and the shock between the kingdom of men and the sovereign government of God. In the initial narratives, God frees his servants and reveals his authority over kings and empires; in later visions, He unfolds the course of history until the final establishment of his Kingdom, the defeat of the oppressive forces, and the resurrection of the righteous. For evangelical readers, the book offers comfort in times of exile, perseverance in holiness and eschatological hope based on the absolute dominion of God.
profile.setting: The main historical scene begins in 605 BC, when Nebuchadnezzar II attacked Jerusalem and took captives to Babylon, among them young people of the royal lineage of Judah. This occurred in the context of God's judgment on his people because of unfaithfulness to the covenant. The exile deepened with new deportations in 597 BC and with the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC, when Judah lost its national condition and appeared absorbed by Babylonian power. The book also reaches 539 BC, when Cyrus of Persia conquered Babylon and allowed the return of the exiles, fulfilling the promise of restoration. As for authorship and date, tradition preserves the attribution to Daniel and sees a strong possibility of writing in the 6th century BC; however, the dating is debated, with later proposals by some scholars. Literarily, the book combines historical narrative, wisdom, and apocalyptic literature, using symbols to reveal God's action behind visible events.

structure.label: Fidelity in the midst of exile
structure.description: Daniel and his companions enter into Babylonish formation, remaining faithful to God as He grants wisdom and preserves his identity.

structure.label: Conflict with the Imperial Power
structure.description: The faithfulness of the captives is tested before a real order contrary to the law of God, and the Lord delivers them.

structure.label: God humbles the pagan sovereign
structure.description: A foreign king receives a revelation interpreted by Daniel, showing that the Most High rules over kings.

structure.label: Fall of pride and new proof
structure.description: Another message to a ruler reveals the judgment of God, and Daniel again stands firm before the opposition.

structure.label: Visions of the course of history and the end of exile
structure.description: The visions present the succession of the kingdoms, the opposition against the people of God, the prayer of Daniel and the revelation of the divine plan to restore his people.

structure.label: Final vision and hope of the resurrection
structure.description: The last view spans future periods of conflict until the consummation of history, culminating in the promise of restoration and resurrection.

themes: The sovereignty of God over kings, empires, and history
Persevering fidelity of God's people on hostile land
Judgment, exile and restoration as acts of the divine covenant
Aescactic hope: eternal kingdom and resurrection
Wisdom and discernment to interpret reality in the light of God
readingKeys: Notice how the narrative chapters show Daniel's faithfulness and at the same time God's decisive action in his behalf.
Read the visions as theological interpretation of history: symbols point to empires, powers, and the destiny of God's people.
Note the repetition of contrasts between human sovereignty and divine sovereignty, especially when kings decree something and God redefines the outcome.
profile.cautions: Some historical and compositional questions remain debated, especially the final date of the book and the way in which its predictions are evaluated. In addition, the book contains the symbolic language of apocalyptic literature; therefore, its images should not be read in a simplistic or isolated way, but in the literary and historical context in which they appear. It is also important to remember that the Protestant tradition does not include certain additions present in the Septuagint and the Vulgate, absent in the Hebrew manuscripts.

dossier.narratedEra: Daniel's narrative setting goes from the first deportation in 605 BC, in the reign of Nebuchadnezzar II, through the decades of Babylonian captivity and the transition to Persian rule, to the restoration linked to Cyrus around 539-535 BC; the narrative itself also opens to visions that reach the "time of the end."
dossier.compositionEra: The annexed notes present two main readings: the traditional one, according to which Daniel would have written the book in the late 500 years BC; and an alternative academic proposal that places the final form around 164 BC, especially because of the accuracy of the predictions of 11:1-35. The sources do not solve the debate, but affirm that Daniel's tradition and authorship are consistent with the character of the book as predictive prophecy.

politics.title: Nebuchadnezzar as an instrument of divine judgment
politics.detail: The notes say that Nebuchadnezzar II of Babylon attacked Jerusalem in 605 BC and took captives, including young people from the royal family of Judah. The Babylonian king appears as an involuntary agent used by the Lord to discipline an unfaithful people to the covenant.
politics.readingImpact: Reading ceases to see exile only as political defeat and begins to see it as theological judgment; Daniel 1 is not only geographical displacement, but the beginning of the judgment and preservation of a remnant.

politics.title: The succession of the great empires: Babylonia, Persia, and beyond
politics.detail: The notes place Babylon as dominant power in the time of Daniel, followed by the Persian ascension under Cyrus. In Daniel 1 and 6, the Babylonian court and then Persian administration shape the plot; in the introduction, the prophetic panorama also reaches Greece and Rome.
politics.readingImpact: The book is read as a story under divine sovereignty, not as an isolated account of individual piety. The change of empire reinforces the theme of which human kingdoms rise and fall, while God governs the course of history.

politics.title: The policy of cutting and the promotion of Daniel
politics.detail: Daniel and his friends were trained to serve in the Babylonian court; then Daniel is promoted to positions of responsibility under successive kings. In Daniel 6, administrators were placed on the territory to protect the royal interests, and the king wanted to raise Daniel over the entire empire.
politics.readingImpact: Daniel's fidelity gains public weight: his integrity is not private, but tested in state structures. The context helps to read your wisdom as a testimony to imperial power.

politics.title: Legal conflict in Persia and the irrevocability of the law
politics.detail: In Daniel 6, the law that forbids prayer is presented as irreversible, a characteristic highlighted in the notes as a special trace of the Persian Empire. The king is imprisoned to his own legislation and official seals, despite recognizing Daniel's innocence.
politics.readingImpact: The scene shows the limit of imperial power: human decrees may seem absolute, but remain subordinate to the living God. This makes the tension between loyalty to the king and loyalty to the Lord more acute.

politics.title: Cyrus and the Return Decree
politics.detail: The notes claim that Cyrus conquered Babylon in 539 BC and allowed the return of the captives, fulfilling Jeremiah. The tradition of the introduction links this decree to the end of the seventy years of servitude and Daniel's prayer in 9:1-19.
politics.readingImpact: The return of exile appears as an act of imperial policy ruled by prophetic promise. Restoration is not born of historical chance, but of God's faithfulness to his time.

customs.title: Formation of courtesan: Babylonian language, literature and science
customs.detail: Daniel and his companions received the best training available at court, including language, literature and science. The notes also describe the vast intellectual production of Babylon, with texts of wisdom, enchantments, history, mathematics and astrology.
customs.readingImpact: This explains why the book values discernment and wisdom: Daniel's fidelity occurs within a very sophisticated pagan educational system, not in cultural isolation.

customs.title: Real table food and risk of ritual contamination
customs.detail: The king's food and wine were seen as potentially unclean to Jews, possibly by including forbidden meats and for being dedicated to Babylonian gods. Daniel asks for vegetables and water, and the notes note that this would also work as a kind of fasting/moment of mourning through exile.
customs.readingImpact: The refusal to feed is not a dietary whim; it marks resistance to religious and moral assimilation. The reader understands better why the gesture is a matter of purity and loyalty.

customs.title: Change of names as assimilation strategy
customs.detail: The four young people receive Babylonian names linked to local deities, replacing the Hebrew names that affirmed the relationship with the God of Israel. The notes say that the change of names was part of a social and religious pressure to absorb them in pagan culture.
customs.readingImpact: The context clarifies that identity and language are in dispute. The reading of Daniel 1 gains density as resistance to the reconfiguration of the identity of the people of God.

customs.title: Administrative life and high social position
customs.detail: Matthew Henry describes Daniel as someone who lived long in the councils and courts of kings, as a cork, a statesman and businessman. Tyndale also shows Daniel being examined and appointed to a relevant position in the kingdom.
customs.readingImpact: The spirituality of the book is neither monastic nor withdrawn from the world; it is exercised at the center of the imperial administration. This guides the reading of historical chapters as a life of faith in public service.

customs.title: Daily Prayer for Jerusalem
customs.detail: In Daniel 6, Daniel maintains his regular prayer schedule and does so with guidance for Jerusalem, a city chosen by God. The notes recall that the temple had disappeared, but Jerusalem remained the center of memory and hope of restoration.
customs.readingImpact: The devotional practice is read as fidelity in the context of national loss. The gesture of praying to Jerusalem connects the exile to God's promise and hope for reconstruction.

customs.title: Fasting, I regret and vigilance in exile
customs.detail: The notes of Daniel 1 and 6 describe practices of abstinence and fasting linked to the suffering of exile, and King Darius spends the night in fasting and sleepless because of Daniel. This background shows how feeding and fasting functioned as bodily signs of distress or devotion.
customs.readingImpact: The body participates in the theology of the book: eating, refusing food, fasting and watching become visible marks of fidelity or mourning. This helps the reader to perceive the concrete dimension of exotic piety.

language.title: Dual language: Hebrew and Aramaic/chaldean
language.detail: Matthew Henry notes that the book alternates Hebrew and the Chaldean/Aramaic dialect: the beginning is in Hebrew, a long central section in Chaldean, and the rest in Hebrew. This is presented as an important literary data of the text itself.
language.readingImpact: The alternation suggests changes in the environment and the public, in addition to marking the passage between cutout reports and prophetic visions. The reader should take this into account before treating the book as homogeneous.
language.reference: Structure of the book; no single versicular reference

language.title: Apocalyptic symbolism: statues, animals and horns
language.detail: The notes of the introduction explain that apocalyptic literature uses symbolic language to represent kings, kingdoms, and people. Daniel 7 is given as an example, with images revealing the reality behind historical events.
language.readingImpact: The interpreter should not read the symbols in a literalistic or arbitrary way. The literary and historical context is necessary to understand the intention of the images.

language.title: The statue and animals as two forms of the same historical plot
language.detail: Tyndale's introduction states that Daniel 7, through animal symbols, tells the same story as Daniel 2: the history of the world culminates in the kingdom of God after strong opposition. Thus, different images communicate the same theological axis.
language.readingImpact: The visions are not disconnected episodes, but literary variations of the same theme: divine sovereignty over empires. This guides the intertextual reading of the book.

language.title: "Son of Man" and the final Kingdom
language.detail: The introduction connects the figure of the Son of Man to New Testament texts and to the eternal reign granted by God. The focus is that the kingdom belongs to God and his people receives him with the King.
language.readingImpact: The language points to eschatological hope and not just for immediate political liberation. The context broadens the reading of visions beyond Babylonian captivity.

language.title: Symbolic numbers and time delimited
language.detail: In Daniel 12, the notes discuss the 1,290 and 1,335 days as numbers possibly linked to events under Antiochus IV Epiphanius, or as symbolic numbers. The text also uses "time, times, and half a time" as a formula of period bounded by God.
language.readingImpact: The reader is warned not to turn the numbers into rigid speculative chronology. The focus lies on the sovereign limit imposed by God on suffering.

language.title: Knowledge, wisdom and light as moral metaphors
language.detail: The notes say that the wise men know God and that He is a common metaphor for life, purity, justice, and glory. In 12:3, this describes the destiny of the faithful and the identity of the wise.
language.readingImpact: Wisdom is not only intellectual capacity; it is moral and relational fidelity. This affects Daniel's reading as a book of spiritual formation, not just prediction.

timeline.title: 605 BC: First deportation with Daniel and his friends
timeline.detail: Tyndale's notes place the initial capture of young people from Judah in 605 BC during Nebuchadnezzar's attack on Jerusalem. This begins the period of Daniel in Babylon.
timeline.readingImpact: The book begins at the point where the promise seems to fail, but precisely there divine fidelity is demonstrated. The setting gives strength to the theme of survival of the holy people in foreign land.

timeline.title: 597 and 586 BC: aggravation of Jerusalem's exile and fall
timeline.detail: The introduction mentions a new deportation in 597 BC and the destruction of Jerusalem in 586 BC. Afterwards, Judah ceases to be an independent nation.
timeline.readingImpact: These milestones broaden the sense of national collapse that surrounds the initial chapters and explain the language of despair and loss. The reader realizes that Daniel acts in the midst of an end of a political order.
timeline.reference: general historical context of the introduction

timeline.title: 539 BC: the fall of Babylon and Persian dominion
timeline.detail: The notes claim that Cyrus invaded Babylon in 539 BC and subdued the city and Belsauzar, according to the prophetic vision associated with Isaiah. This leads to the change of power that appears in Daniel 5-6 and the subsequent restoration.
timeline.readingImpact: The imperial turn confirms the theme that arrogant kingdoms are not definitive. Daniel's reading must accompany this transition as a concrete demonstration of divine sovereignty.

timeline.title: End of exile and return under Cyrus
timeline.detail: The introduction states that the return decree fulfills Jeremiah and occurs after about seventy years of servitude. Daniel 9 is linked to this restoration through his prayer in the same year and the angelic response.
timeline.readingImpact: Daniel's prayer is not abstract devotional, but is tied to the historical unfolding of the restoration. The context shows the relationship between prophecy, prayer and political change.

timeline.title: Third year of Cyrus and the final vision
timeline.detail: The introduction situates the last bloc of visions from the third year of Cyrus (536 BC), with a horizon that goes to Greece, Rome and the resurrection. The note of 12:13 also guarantees Daniel a future resurrection.
timeline.readingImpact: The book moves from historical exile to eschatological hope. The reader should interpret the latest visions as a broad panorama of history and the end, not as a mere record of immediate crises.

investigation: The traditional authorship is attributed to Daniel, but the notes recognize the academic debate about a final essay in the 2nd century BC; the source insists that the internal attribution of the book to Daniel is an important part of the discussion.
There are historical gaps and some historical problems mentioned by the notes, but they do not detail which are beyond the general discussion about date and the accuracy of 11:1-35.
The book is treated as predictive prophecy and also as apocalyptic literature; notes recommend interpreting symbols from the text itself and the available historical context.

The coverage of the notes is selective: some aspects of Daniel 7-12 are summarized only in general terms, and references to the Greek and Roman period appear in a panoramic way, without detailed chronology.
Matthew Henry mentions ancient traditions and rabbinical opinions on Daniel's status, but this reflects confessional and ancient historical reading, not modern academic consensus.
dossier.limits: This dossier uses only the attached notes and therefore does not attempt to harmonise internal differences or fill gaps with external knowledge. The sources offer good coverage about exile, Babylonian court, Persian transition, apocalyptic language and authorship/date; however, they treat the later chronology, the exact identification of some characters and the extent of certain visions. There are also explicitly debated points, such as the final date of the book, the meaning of some numbers in Daniel 12 and the reading of 11:1-35. Where the notes interpret, this was marked as interpretation; where they record dispute, as debated; and where they affirm something directly, as explicit-source.
